b161.content:
A devout Catholic Highlander and a fiery atheist agree to fight a duel over religion, but the police, the press, and the whole modern world keep interrupting them.

As they flee across England, the two enemies become friends. The novel is full of Chesterton’s paradoxes and humor.

b162.content:
Written a few years after his own reception into the Church in 1922, Chesterton’s short book describes the stages a person goes through in approaching the Catholic faith: first patronizing it, then discovering it, and finally running from it, before surrendering.

It is a witty, honest account of why so many thoughtful people were becoming Catholic.

b163.content:
Ronald Knox, an Anglican clergyman who became a Catholic priest, explains with clarity and wit why he believes what the Catholic Church teaches, from the existence of God to the authority of the Church.

It was one of the most effective works of 20th-century English apologetics.

b164.content:
The German-Italian priest Romano Guardini analyzes how the modern age, with its confidence in nature, the autonomous individual, and culture, is giving way to something new: an age of mass society and immense technological power without a corresponding growth in conscience.

Pope Francis quoted it extensively in Laudato Si’.

b165.content:
Josefa Menéndez was a Spanish lay sister of the Society of the Sacred Heart who died at thirty-three in 1923. Her superiors recorded the messages she reported receiving from Christ about His Sacred Heart and His mercy toward sinners.

Published after her death, the book became a classic of 20th-century devotion to the Sacred Heart.

b166.content:
Thérèse’s letters to her sisters, her cousins, and two missionary priests she adopted as spiritual brothers show the Little Way in action, in her own words and without the editing of her autobiography.

They reveal her humor, her suffering during her final illness, and her unshakable trust in God’s merciful love.

b167.content:
One of the most widely read books of the early Church, the Shepherd records visions given to Hermas, a former slave in Rome, by a woman representing the Church and by an angel in the form of a shepherd.

Its great theme is repentance: after Baptism, sinners may still return to God through a second repentance. Some early Christians even read it alongside Scripture, though the Church did not include it in the canon.

b168.content:
A short, elegant letter by an unknown Christian to an inquiring pagan named Diognetus, explaining why Christians reject idols and Jewish sacrifices and why they love one another.

Its most famous passage describes Christians as the soul of the world: living in every country as citizens, yet as foreigners, obeying the laws while surpassing them by their lives.

b169.content:
A letter from the church of Smyrna describing the arrest and death of its aged bishop, St. Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John. Urged to curse Christ, he answered that he had served him for eighty-six years and that Christ had never done him wrong.

It is the oldest surviving account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament, and the first to speak of keeping the anniversary of a martyr’s death and honoring his relics.

b170.content:
Polycarp wrote to the church at Philippi, which had asked him for the letters of St. Ignatius of Antioch. He encourages them to faith, righteousness, and patience, and warns against greed and false teaching.

The letter is full of echoes of the New Testament and shows how early the apostolic writings were known and treasured.

b171.content:
Justin recounts his conversion from philosophy to Christ and a long debate with a Jewish teacher named Trypho in Ephesus.

He argues from the Old Testament that Jesus is the Messiah foretold by the prophets, and he gives one of the earliest descriptions of Mary as the new Eve, whose obedience undid Eve’s disobedience.

b172.content:
Three books addressed by the bishop of Antioch to a pagan friend, explaining the Christian faith in one Creator and defending the Scriptures against pagan myths.

Theophilus is the first known writer to use the Greek word for "Trinity" (trias) of God, his Word, and his Wisdom.

b173.content:
Much of this account was written by Perpetua herself, a young noblewoman and nursing mother of Carthage, in prison as she awaited martyrdom with her slave Felicity and other catechumens.

She records her visions and her father’s pleas, making it one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. An editor completed it with the story of their deaths in the arena.

b174.content:
Clement, head of the catechetical school of Alexandria, presents Christ as the divine Teacher who trains his children in a life of virtue.

The work gives detailed and often surprising advice on eating, drinking, clothing, conversation, and the use of wealth, and ends with one of the oldest surviving Christian hymns.

b175.content:
A sermon on the rich young man of Mark 10. Clement argues that wealth itself is not condemned; what matters is detachment of the heart and generous use of riches for others.

It closes with the moving story of the apostle John seeking out a young man who had become a robber and bringing him back to Christ.

b176.content:
The first attempt at a systematic Christian theology, covering God, the Trinity, creation, rational beings, free will, and the interpretation of Scripture.

Origen was a brilliant and devout teacher, but some of his speculations, such as the pre-existence of souls, were later rejected by the Church. The work is still important for its method of reading Scripture on several levels.

b177.content:
A point-by-point reply to The True Word, an attack on Christianity by the pagan philosopher Celsus.

Origen answers charges that Christians were ignorant and credulous, defends the miracles and Resurrection of Jesus, and points to the changed lives of Christians as evidence of the truth of the faith.

b178.content:
Written during a schism in Rome and Carthage after the persecution of Decius, this treatise insists that there is one Church, founded on Peter, and that no one can separate from it without leaving Christ.

It contains Cyprian’s famous image of the Church as the mother of all believers, and his teaching that the unity of the Church is like the seamless garment of Christ, which could not be torn.

b179.content:
A beautiful commentary on the Our Father, phrase by phrase, written for the Christians of Carthage.

Cyprian explains that we pray in the plural because we are one people, and that "our daily bread" refers both to ordinary food and to Christ in the Eucharist.

b180.content:
The African writer Tertullian argues that heretics have no right even to use the Scriptures, because the Scriptures belong to the Church that received them from the apostles.

The true faith can be found in the churches founded by the apostles, with their unbroken lines of bishops. Tertullian later joined the Montanist sect, but this work remained influential.

b181.content:
The earliest surviving treatise on any of the sacraments. Tertullian explains why water was chosen for Baptism, describes the rite and its anointing and laying on of hands, and answers those who said faith alone was enough.

It gives a valuable picture of how Christians were initiated around the year 200.

b182.content:
A graceful Latin dialogue set on the beach at Ostia, in which the Christian Octavius answers his pagan friend Caecilius, who has blown a kiss to a statue of Serapis.

Octavius refutes the slanders spread about Christians and argues for one God and the resurrection. At the end, Caecilius is persuaded and becomes a Christian.

b183.content:
Lactantius, a famous teacher of rhetoric, wrote this first Latin summary of Christian belief during the Great Persecution, to show educated pagans that Christianity is true wisdom and true religion.

He was later tutor to the son of Constantine, and his elegant style earned him the nickname "the Christian Cicero."

b184.content:
The first history of the Church, from the apostles to the victory of Constantine. Eusebius lists the bishops of the great churches, describes the martyrs, and quotes many early writings that would otherwise be lost.

Almost everything we know about the Church of the second and third centuries depends in part on this book.

b185.content:
Athanasius’s great defense of the Council of Nicaea’s teaching that the Son is "of one substance" with the Father.

He answers the Arians’ favorite proof texts one by one and shows that if the Son were a creature, he could not make us sharers in the divine nature. Only God can save.

b186.content:
A prologue and twenty-three lectures given in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre to those preparing for Baptism at Easter and to the newly baptized.

The first eighteen explain the Creed of Jerusalem. The last five, the Mystagogical Lectures, explain Baptism, Chrismation, and the Eucharist, and they are a clear witness to the early Church’s belief in the Real Presence.

b187.content:
Five sermons preached in Constantinople, which earned Gregory the title "the Theologian." He defends the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit and explains how God can be one and three.

They were decisive for the Council of Constantinople in 381, which completed the Nicene Creed.

b188.content:
Nine Lenten homilies on the six days of creation in Genesis, preached by Basil to the working people of Caesarea.

Basil delights in the beauty and order of nature, from fish and birds to the stars, and draws moral and spiritual lessons from each creature, leading his listeners to praise the Creator.

b189.content:
A handbook for teachers of the faith, explaining the Trinity, the Incarnation, Baptism, and the Eucharist and answering the objections of pagans and Jews.

Gregory explains why God became man and how Christ’s Body in the Eucharist unites believers to his immortal life.

b190.content:
Written to complete his brother Basil’s Hexaemeron, this treatise reflects on the creation of human beings in the image of God.

Gregory explores the dignity of the human person as a "royal" creature made to rule creation, the unity of soul and body, and the destiny of humanity in the resurrection.

b191.content:
Gregory recounts a conversation with his dying sister, St. Macrina, whom he calls "the Teacher." Grieving for their brother Basil, he asks her about death, the soul, and the resurrection of the body.

It is a Christian answer to Plato’s Phaedo, and a moving portrait of one of the wisest women of the early Church.

b192.content:
Gregory first retells the story of Moses and then reads it as an allegory of the soul’s journey to God: from the light of the burning bush, through the cloud, to the darkness of Mount Sinai where God is found beyond all concepts.

Its teaching that the spiritual life is endless progress has shaped mystics East and West.

b193.content:
Ambrose explains to the newly baptized the meaning of the rites they had just received at the Easter Vigil: the opening of the ears, Baptism, the anointing, and the Eucharist.

He teaches clearly that the words of Christ change the bread and wine into his Body and Blood. Ambrose had baptized St. Augustine a few years earlier.

b194.content:
Modeled on Cicero’s On Duties, this work was written for the priests of Milan but became the first Christian handbook of ethics.

Ambrose discusses prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance in the light of Scripture, and teaches that the Church’s wealth exists to ransom captives and feed the poor.

b195.content:
Ambrose wrote this work for his sister Marcellina, who had received the veil of a consecrated virgin from Pope Liberius.

He praises consecrated virginity and holds up the Virgin Mary as its model, describing her humility, modesty, and love of prayer.

b196.content:
Written while Hilary was exiled to Asia Minor for opposing Arianism, this was the first great Latin work on the Trinity.

Hilary defends the true divinity of the Son and ends with a heartfelt prayer that he may always confess the Father and the Son. It earned him the title "the Athanasius of the West."

b197.content:
Ephrem, the "Harp of the Spirit," wrote these Syriac hymns for the feast of Christ’s birth. They marvel at the paradox of the Incarnation: the Creator nursing at his mother’s breast, the Ancient of Days as a little child.

Mary herself often speaks in the hymns, singing to her Son. They are among the most beautiful poetry of the early Church.

b198.content:
Twenty-three short treatises written in Syriac by a monk-bishop in the Persian Empire, outside the Roman world.

Aphrahat writes on faith, love, fasting, prayer, humility, and the "sons of the covenant," an early form of consecrated life. His work shows Christianity in its Semitic, non-Greek form.

b199.content:
Ninety sermons preached in Antioch, among the greatest commentaries on Matthew from the early Church.

Chrysostom, "the golden-mouthed," moves easily from explaining the text to challenging his congregation about wealth, the poor, the theatre, and the Eucharist. His call to see Christ in the poor is as sharp today as it was then.

b200.content:
When riots broke out in Antioch and the people tore down statues of the emperor and his family, the whole city feared terrible punishment.

During the anxious weeks of Lent that followed, the young priest John preached these twenty-one sermons, comforting the people, calling them to repentance, and preaching against swearing oaths, while their bishop traveled to Constantinople to plead for mercy.
